column97:
My choices are affected by a trick-or-treating history in a small northern town, where the following formative observations were made:
(1) almost nobody ever gave out those little chocolate bars (has resulted in hoarding and overindulgence in these as an adult)
(2) sunflower seeds in the shell were cheap and therefore popular. I believe my record was 17 bags one year. Everyone brought them to school the day after, because they'd finished the (small amount of) good candy already.
(3) similar story with the little black-and-orange wrapped toffee things. Honestly, I'm not sure anyone ever ate them; suspect they just made the rounds year after year. I know my parents would snag ours to give out to the late trick-or-treaters after they'd run out of whatever they'd bought that year.
(4) in a small town the homemade T&T treats are OK to keep - but they'd come with the maker's name and address to make sure. 
(5) cash not evocative of joy as it always went in the little Unicef boxes
(6) we knew about the razorblade apple stories but were innocent of the concept of toothbrushes or pencils going in the trick-or-treat bags - that would have scarred us for life.

column97:
I appreciate and thoroughly enjoy the work being done here.  Candy, through no fault of it's own other than being dentally devastating, is increasingly losing it's rightful place atop the American Totem Pole.  That being said, I do have some qualms with this study.  3 key schisms have been mysteriously left out.  They are: Freshness, Presentation, and Saturation of the Market.

Freshness is pretty self explanatory.  If any of the above items I marked as "Joy" are from a previous year's Halloween, then they will always cause despair.  There are few exceptions to this rule, one of which will be explained in item 3.

Presentation is also one of candy's basic fundamentals.  Passing out loose candy is a cardinal sin.  All treats need to be wrapped, boxed or hermetically sealed.  Those who fashion unique edible arrangements in hopes of delighting children are the worst of these offenders.  While I appreciate your skill in arts and crafts and admire your desire to be different, please note: unboxed Junior Mints will always ruin my pillow case.

Saturation of the Market is a bit tougher to nail down.  This comes from more of an Obscurist perspective.  Store bought candy, while containing popular favorites from recognized brands, is in great abundance come All Hallows Eve.  True Trick or Treaters know the value of a rare, undiscovered, or discontinued candy (this is the exception noted above).  I will sacrifice taste and comfort for a new more visceral experience.  While Butterfingers do offer a delectable flavor explosion each time you devour one, a tart and chalky bottle of Bug City will make that Halloween unforgettable.

column97:
When I was a about 8 my father took me hunting for the first time for deer.  I remember how his childhood rifle felt in my hand, heavy with memories, mortality, and steel.  I remember his rough hands on my shoulders as I shot cans off the fence that ran around our property; each shot closer to the mark than the last.  Finally, with the ringing sound of five cans slain he took the gun from my trembling hands and said "son you're a man now, let the hunt begin".  He packed two sandwiches and four beers in a small, lined rucksack, grabbed the blood-crusted oilskin he used to haul back his kill, and then we began the five mile hike to his hunting blind somewhere in the woods on the edge of our property.  The cans lay on the ground, jittering slightly in that icy, pre-dawn breeze; the holes I had shot in them whistling slightly.  I will never forget that high, faint whistling.

We'd been walking for about an hour, and the sun had begun to creep above the horizon, percolating down through the dense forest canopy.  We hadn't seen many deer, but we also hadn't been looking.  Suddenly I heard the sound of rustling behind us.  My father, ever the experienced huntsman, pulled his old Winchester from his bag.  In one, fluid motion he had loaded it and stepped between me and the noise.  Everything went silent for the span of a heartbeat, and then out from the low bushes tumbled a small bear, about my size.  My heart melted and I let out an "awww!".  Pushing past my father I had time to register his scream "NO" before it was cut short by a roar that sounded like the end of the world.  From behind the baby grizzly bear stepped its mother: a 10 foot behemoth with claws the size of my longest finger.  In an instant it pulled back a mighty paw.  I remember the smell of my father's hunting vest as he pulled my face into his chest, and I remember how quickly it disappeared when he was struck by the bear.  My father was a large man, but that blow sent him sailing through the air like the cans I had shot earlier.  He landed with a terrible thud.  I screamed.  The bear began to charge at him.

On the ground, at my feet, lay his Winchester.  Without thinking I grabbed it and shot the bear.  I've heard stories from old men say that an enraged mother bear won't even notice being shot by a rifle, but this bear certainly did.  "No no no!" I heard my father moan as the bear wheeled back on me.

Everything stopped again.  I could hear the bear snuffling.  I could see it's breath in the icy air, and I could see the steam rising from my father's bleeding body.  The gun was heavy in my hand, and it reeked with the acrid burn of gunpowder.  I raised it to my cheek, as my father had taught me that morning.  There was no tremor in my as I looked the bear square in the eyes and squeezed the trigger.

The sound it made as it's carcass hit the ground was enough to bring the fear screaming back into my heart.  My knees buckled and I cried for my father.  The baby bear scrambled back into the foliage.  Though I couldn't see through the hot tears, I heard my father pull himself up off the ground and stumble towards me.  The hot tears on my face mixed with the hot blood on his hands as he held my face for a moment.  "Oh my son," he said "you were already a man in my eyes, you should have let me die."

"Why father?"

"Because we hunt deers for food, and bears hunt us for food.  It is the natural way of things.  And now I must teach you this."

The walk home was a blur of shock and fading adrenaline.  My feet felt like lead in my boots, and several times I had to stop and vomit until eventually my stomach ran dry.  I remember the creak of the barn door and the dry must of the old, October hay.

"Come, sit on this stool," said my father, so I did.  He stood in front of me, a long sock in one hand and a bag of candy corn in the other.

"For food to strike what eats it is an offense to God," he said.  "Now I will teach you this."  I watched as he poured the candy corn into the sock.  I didn't yell when he struck me in the face with it.  As the blood-sodden mass of waxy candy drummed the natural order of the world into my young body, I reflected back on the baby bear.  I knew it would die alone, and so I began to cry.  My father did not mistake these tears for weakness.  Instead the blows paused for a brief moment.  "Oh my son," he said.  "Oh my sweet son."  And the blows continued.

In summary: to this day the taste of candy corn reminds me of the smell of hay.
